chapter_theme: The Vidyadhara kings and the gods gather for Civakan's crowning; he is bathed, crowned and seated on the lion throne, and his first orders as king, given through his brother and the royal drum, restore the temples' and Brahmins' lands, remit dues, and promise help to the hungry, the sick and the abandoned before the narrator turns to the next ilampakam.

cast.role: Civakan's younger brother (தம்பி), who carries out the king's orders
the Vidyadhara kings who gather for the crowning
the god who descends and crowns Civakan
the heavenly women who descend and sing
the beings who appear in the sky (taken as gods)
the guardian kings allied to Civakan
the people of the land who live under Civakan

2361.reading: The Vidyadhara kings of the silver mountain leave it and gather in Civakan's city in such numbers that they look like the moon's scattered rays drawn together.
2361.event: The Vidyadhara kings come down from Vellimalai and assemble in the city.

2362.reading: Someone urges that there is nothing more to consider, that he should resolve to put on the fine crown and that the lord and the assembly should come, while a crown set with gems is made ready on the god-like hero's head.
2362.nuance: Lines 1-2 are an exhortation in the imperative, but the verse does not name who speaks or who கண்ணனார் is; lines 3-4 are hard to construe.
2362.event: The assembled kings press Civakan to be crowned and a gem-set crown is prepared.

2363.reading: A god with a flowing garland, a shining crown and a jewelled chest-ornament swaying descends, trembling like a golden hill.
2363.nuance: Which god is meant is not said; the Cintamani's gods who attend Civakan are not named here.
2363.event: A god comes down from the sky for the crowning.

2364.reading: Heavenly women with full breasts, bright jewelled strings and soft hair come down like flashes of lightning from a rain-cloud.
2364.event: Celestial women descend in a procession.

2365.reading: Fierce-looking beings arrive in the sky in splendour, bringing a scent of the divine city that drowns the scent of the rutting elephants of the king's city.
2365.nuance: வெய்யர் (the fierce or hot ones) is taken to be the gods of the sky; the verse does not say so.
2365.event: More heavenly beings arrive in the sky above the city.

2366.reading: The citizens, frightened, clap in wonder; with rains of flowers and gold he bathes Civakan with a hundred and eight pots of water from the milk sea and places the bright gold crown on him, worshipping.
2366.nuance: The subject of கவித்தனன் is not named; it is taken to be the god who came down in 2363. The crown is given by heavenly hands, not by a priest or an elder king.
2366.event: A god bathes Civakan with water from the milk sea and sets the golden crown on his head.

2367.reading: Divine drums sound to announce it to the gods, apsaras praise with the vina's sound and smoke and powder rise, and the guardian kings and the assembly do what is due.
2367.event: The apsaras sing and the kings and assembly carry out the rites of the crowning.

2368.reading: A white umbrella rises like the full moon over a pole of gems, and the god who has risen to bless is joined with the matchless Earth-goddess, the king who now guards the sea-girt land.
2368.nuance: The verse is built from similes and its last line, where the god rises and joins பூமகள், is ambiguous: it may mean Civakan taking the land as his bride or the god's blessing on it. The ilampakam is named for பூமகள்.
2368.event: Civakan, crowned, is joined to the goddess of earth as ruler of the land.

2369.reading: With white fly-whisks waving, a golden umbrella shading him and kings bowing to take his feet, he goes forth in state, praised by women of sweet speech, like Vishnu.
2369.event: Civakan goes in procession to the throne hall, with kings bowing to his feet.

2370.reading: He enters the picture-hall, set with the gem called cintamani, a hall that only the lotus goddess of fortune, and no other woman, has entered.
2370.event: Civakan enters the painted hall of the throne.

2371.reading: He sits on the lion throne, among kings in their crowns, like a lion, with his earrings flashing, like the sun shining from a dark cloud.
2371.event: Civakan takes his seat on the lion throne in the midst of the kings.

2372.reading: Looking at his younger brother, Civakan bids him clear the afflictions of the towns and the districts and have the war-drum proclaim that the land his enemy ruled is rid of the stain of its burden.
2372.nuance: The enemy's land is described by பிணி (bond or disease) in each half-line; the drum is the royal drum used for orders. The pun is not fixed.
2372.event: Civakan orders his brother to relieve the towns of their afflictions and to proclaim it by drum.

2373.reading: He commands that the lands of the temples, the lands of the learned who read the stars, and the fire-places and fields of the four-Veda Brahmins, taken from them, be given back twofold.
2373.nuance: The seizure is not told in these verses; the 'losers' are the gods' shrines, the astrologers and the Brahmins, so the order is also the work's picture of whom a Jain king should protect.
2373.event: Civakan orders land taken from temples and Brahmins to be restored at double.

claims.claim: A king who finds lands taken from the gods' places and the learned must restore them twofold

2374.reading: Hearing him, the brother bows, touches the ground with his head, has the victorious drum set on a tall elephant and, through the old city of flagged mansions, has the drum of the lord proclaimed.
2374.event: Nandattan has the royal drum carried on an elephant through the city to proclaim the orders.

2375.reading: The drum announces that the king has remitted the dues for sixteen years and that those who are alive should live together, and that hunger, disease and enmity should perish.
2375.nuance: பதிளை யாண்டை is read as sixteen years; the number is not certain, and the reading of குறுகடன் as 'dues' is a guess.
2375.event: The drum proclaims remission of dues and the end of hunger, disease and enmity.

claims.claim: A king's reign is to be marked by remission of dues and the ending of hunger, disease and enmity

2376.reading: The drum goes on to those blind, wasted with disease, women left by the husbands who married them, and others cast out, that the stored wealth will be given so that they may live, and the king has it sounded through the city.
2376.event: The king has the drum proclaim that his wealth will support the blind, the sick, abandoned wives and the cast out.

claims.claim: A king owes the helpless, the sick and the abandoned a share of the treasury

2377.reading: The narrator says that, by the grace of Civakan the people live in gladness like one wife to one man, with enemies, disease and hunger gone, and that he will now tell what befell the king of kings.
2377.nuance: The last line turns from the praise of Civakan's rule to the next ilampakam; the story it opens ends in the king's renunciation, as the patikam (verse 27) says.
2377.event: The people live at ease and the narrator moves on to what happened to the king of kings.

links.note: The patikam opens with Saccandan, king of the unbending sceptre; Civakan's first order from the throne is to clear his realm of afflictions and have the drum announce it.
links.teaches: The son's first act as king is the sceptre's work that his father's reign set at the start, so the epic sets his crowning as the repair of the wrong the story began with.

links.note: The patikam says that Civakan renounces while kings bring tribute and his sceptre runs just; this verse ends the ilampakam on the people's peace and turns to what befell the king of kings.
links.teaches: The peace of 2377 is the height from which the patikam says he turns away, so the praise of his rule is the setup for the renunciation, not the end of the tale.

links.note: Kural 390 names giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people as the four that make a king a light; the proclamation of 2375 turns them into acts: remission of dues and the end of hunger, disease and enmity.
links.teaches: The couplet's four virtues become a single proclamation with named relief, which shows what giving and care of the people cost a treasury and who is to benefit.

gains.a: The proclamation gains a standard by which its remission and the ending of hunger are measured as the work of a king.
gains.b: The couplet gains concrete acts, a remitted tax, for virtues it only names.

links.note: Kural 557 says a king's lack of grace is for those who live what the lack of rain is for the earth; 2376 has the king's wealth go as grace to the blind, the sick and the wives abandoned.
links.teaches: The couplet states the cost of a king's lack of grace in the language of rain, while the epic names those who would be left dry, showing who counts as the people the sceptre owes.

gains.a: The proclamation gains the couplet's picture of grace as rain: help that reaches those who cannot ask.
gains.b: The couplet gains named sufferers, the blind, the sick and the abandoned wife, who are the dry land of its simile.

links.note: Naladiyar 3 says that even kings who rode in state under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 2371 seats the victor on the lion throne in the full pomp of such a king, after the usurper's fall.
links.teaches: The throne scene stands on the ground the quatrain describes: the pomp the winner now enjoys is what the usurper lost, so the crowning is shown as one turn of a wheel, not a rest.

gains.a: The enthronement gains a warning that the seat is held only while deeds support it.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which the fallen king's rival, not death, is the agent of the fall.

links.note: In 2366 a god crowns Civakan with gold and sea-water; Tirumanthiram 1601 says that those who rule the three worlds wear crowns, but the bliss of the kings of the Lord's feet has no measure.
links.teaches: The Cintamani lets the crowning be the height of splendour, while the Saiva verse ranks the same crowned kings below those who serve at the feet, so what counts as the highest state is exactly what the two texts divide on.

gains.a: The coronation gains a rival measure of rank, in which crowns do not count, against which its splendour can be weighed.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a full scene of a crowned king receiving the highest earthly honour, so its contrast has a concrete case.

source_issues: 2361-2377 were printed in eight half-lines in most verses and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2375 line 1 பதிளை யாண்டைக் குறுகடன் is obscure; 'sixteen years' is taken from பதிளை and is not certain.
2368 line 4 and 2362 lines 1-2 are hard to construe.
